title: Cold Storage
subtitle: EHR Storage Failure & Downtime Continuity

brief.userPrompt: Tuesday, February 9, 2027, a cold night in Duluth. At 02:10 a storage controller fault at the primary data center makes the Lakechart database unavailable; clinicians see spinning screens, the IS Help Desk (ext. 5500) takes the first calls at 02:14 and on-call analyst Ananya Desai confirms at 02:25 that the EHR and the interface engine are both down and that replication to the Hermantown secondary was 40 minutes behind. The exercise starts at 02:40 with the Administrator on Call and Night House Supervisor, 98 inpatients in house, 22 patients in the ED and a woman in active labor. Marcus Ellery (Clinical Systems Lead) and CMIO Dr. Priya Raman are on their way. The target is every unit on downtime procedures within 60 minutes of declaration; the plan's downtime level (3 or 4) turns on whether Gregory Pruitt, the Privacy and Security Officer, can rule out a security cause, and at 03:30 the managed security provider reports an unrelated odd login on a service account that muddies the picture until 06:15. Pressure points: the declaration and the overhead page; units that are slow to report; the downtime viewer is 3 hours 20 minutes old; a critical potassium of 6.9 and a positive blood culture phoned by the lab (Tomas Nygaard) that need read-back inside 60 minutes; the ICU wants pump and monitor network isolation; override pulls in the automated dispensing cabinets and a controlled-substance count mismatch for Pharmacy Operations Manager Alicia Voss; unidentified trauma patients registered as ZZ-Trauma Tuesday 1 and 2 and a possible overlay between two patients named Carlson on the medical-surgical unit; the EHR vendor's priority-one line, which promises a callback in 30 minutes and does not call for 55; the interface engine vendor's on-call engineer, who calls back in about 2 hours; at 06:00 the standby engine is promoted and 31,000 queued messages must be dispositioned (replay, hold or discard) by class, including stale orders for discharged patients; the restore order against the clinician priority list (identity check, lab interface, EHR, pharmacy interface) and a request from the ED medical director to open the EHR before the lab interface is validated; the EHR restore is estimated for about 14:00, after ENDEX, when units will report reconciliation counts hourly and the HIM Director (Janelle Brandt) will track duplicates; the question of whether this is a reportable breach and when the 60-day clock would start; staff and the public hear about it, and a local TV reporter and a post on a community Facebook group claim that the hospital has been hacked, so Hannah Lindqvist (PIO) must keep statements consistent with what is known. The SimCell plays the EHR vendor, the interface engine vendor, the lab and radiology and pharmacy system vendors, the regional health information exchange, the Minnesota Department of Health, the St. Louis County ambulance dispatch, a neighboring hospital, the cyber insurer's breach coach, reporters and families.
audience: Night House Supervisor / Chief Nursing Officer
constraints: Every email address of the hospital uses the exercise domain lakemonthospital.example; vendors and outside parties use fictional *.example domains; never a real hospital, vendor or newspaper domain; phone numbers are 218-555-01xx.

Use the plan's downtime levels, the 60-minute targets and the restore priority list as written; paper forms are the downtime forms named in the SOP (order set, requisition, Critical Result Call Log, downtime medication log); no real patient data, only synthetic names.
Player roles are only those in the audience list; the EHR and interface vendors, the HIE, the state, neighbors, the insurer, reporters and families are played by the SimCell.

overview.theme: Declaring the right downtime level fast when a security cause can't yet be ruled out, keeping patients safe on paper overnight, restoring in a safe order without a chart that looks complete but isn't, and speaking publicly about a failure that people are calling a hack.
overview.threat: On Tuesday, February 9, 2027, at 02:10, before STARTEX, a storage controller failed at the primary data center and the Lakechart (EHR) database went down. There was no attacker. The IS Help Desk (ext. 5500) took the first calls at 02:14. At 02:25 on-call analyst Ananya Desai confirmed that both the EHR and the interface engine were down and that replication to the Hermantown secondary was 40 minutes behind. With the engine down, ADT, orders, results, medication administration, charges and the outbound public health and HIE feeds are queuing in their source systems and can only be held for up to 8 hours. At 03:30 the managed security provider reports an unrelated odd login on a service account. Until 06:15 it is unclear whether this is Level 3 or Level 4.
overview.operationalImpact: The exercise starts at 02:40 on a cold night. 98 inpatients are in house, 22 patients are in the ED and a woman is in active labor. Clinicians see spinning Lakechart screens. The read-only downtime viewer is 3 hours 20 minutes old, so every downtime report is stale by its as-of time. Charge nurses wait for the overhead page and the House Supervisor's call, and slow units must be chased to report when they went on procedures. Unit clerks and registration staff switch to paper. In the ED, two unidentified trauma patients are registered as ZZ-Trauma Tuesday 1 and 2, and on the medical-surgical unit two patients named Carlson may share one record (an overlay). Laboratory technologists keep the analyzers running, print results and phone them. A critical potassium of 6.9 and a positive blood culture each need a read-back and a log entry within 60 minutes. Pharmacy technologists face override pulls from the automated dispensing cabinets and a controlled-substance count that doesn't match. Biomedical technicians get an ICU request to isolate the pump and monitor network. EHR analysts and interface analysts wait 55 minutes for an EHR vendor callback that was promised in 30, and about 2 hours for the interface engine vendor's on-call engineer. At 06:00 they promote the standby engine and must decide, class by class, whether to replay, hold or discard 31,000 queued messages, including stale orders for discharged patients. The ED medical director asks to open the EHR before the lab interface has been validated. The exercise ends before the roughly 14:00 restore of the EHR; the hourly reconciliation counts and duplicate tracking by the HIM Director that follow are covered in the hot wash. Throughout, families ask what is happening at the bedside. Staff, a local TV reporter and a post in a community Facebook group say the hospital has been hacked, and the PIO has to keep every statement consistent with what is actually known.

objectives.name: Decision Making
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to declare and later revise the Lakechart downtime level, choosing between Level 3 and Level 4 while the 03:30 service-account login is unexplained, and to decide within 2 hours, with the ED Medical Director, whether to divert elective admissions or ambulances.

objectives.name: Use of Doctrine
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to put every unit on paper downtime procedures within 60 minutes of the overhead page and to keep patients safe on paper, including phoning the critical potassium of 6.9 and the positive blood culture with read-back and a Critical Result Call Log entry within 60 minutes, and holding the ZZ-Trauma and Carlson identities apart.

objectives.name: Technical Analysis
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to sequence the restore and decide, message class by message class, whether to replay, hold or discard the 31,000 queued messages under IS-14-C section 2 (ADT first, decisions logged), and to refuse to open Lakechart to clinicians before the lab results interface is validated.

objectives.name: Communication
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to issue staff, family and media statements that are cleared by the Incident Commander and match what is known, including a holding statement that answers the 'hospital was hacked' claims from staff, a local TV reporter and a community Facebook post without confirming or ruling out a security cause before the Privacy and Security Officer decides.

roles.name: Downtime Incident Commander (Administrator on Call)
roles.team: Team A: Administrator on Call / Incident Commander
roles.description: Owns the downtime declaration and level, opens the Boardroom command center, makes the diversion decision with the ED Medical Director, and declares return to normal until handing command to the CMIO.
standingOrders: Declare Early: declare a level on the facts you have, then change it; an undeclared downtime is the worst level.
Assume Hostile: if a security cause cannot be ruled out within 60 minutes, run the event as a suspected security incident, even if it slows the restore.
Clinicians Wait: no one opens Lakechart to clinicians until ADT and results have caught up and been validated, however senior the person asking.
One Voice: every public and staff statement goes through you before release.

roles.name: Director of Clinical Informatics (Clinical Systems Lead)
roles.description: Manages the technical recovery with the EHR and interface engine vendors, logs vendor case numbers, and proposes the restore order and the replay, hold or discard decision for each message class.
standingOrders: Log It: put every vendor case number, callback time and discard decision (class, count, who decided) on the command board.
ADT First: restore registration before orders and results so that no result lands on the wrong patient or on no patient.
Escalate the Clock: when a vendor misses its promised callback, escalate at once; the queues can be held for 8 hours at most.
Preserve Evidence: do not wipe or rebuild the failed storage until the Privacy and Security Officer says you may.

roles.name: Nursing House Supervisor / Chief Nursing Officer
roles.team: Team C: Night House Supervisor / Chief Nursing Officer
roles.description: Owns unit readiness and the Nursing paper workflow overnight, calls each charge nurse, chases units that have not reported, and keeps the running count of lost, delayed or duplicated orders and results.
standingOrders: Chase Silence: call any unit that has not reported it is on procedures after 15 minutes.

Trust the Armband: when the downtime viewer or a report disagrees with the patient in front of you, believe the patient and the armband, and remember every report is only as current as its as-of time.
Double Check: every high-alert medication given on paper gets an independent check by a second nurse, whatever the staffing.

roles.name: Laboratory Manager and Pharmacy Operations Manager
roles.team: Team D: Laboratory and Pharmacy Managers
roles.description: Owns the LIS, the critical result call list, the pharmacy system, the dispensing cabinet override, and the Downtime Medication Log, and reports the manual state of each within 30 minutes.
standingOrders: Phone Criticals: phone every critical result with read-back and log it within 60 minutes; never rely on a printout or an email.
Count Controls: report any mismatch in the controlled-substance count at once instead of reconciling it quietly.
Validate Before Release: do not allow the lab interface to feed Lakechart until a sample of results matches the analyzer and the patient, even if the ED is pushing.

roles.name: Privacy and Security Officer
roles.team: Team E: Privacy and Security Officer
roles.description: Owns the decision on whether the outage is a security incident, which systems may reconnect, and the HIPAA four-factor breach risk assessment with its notification clocks and decision log.
standingOrders: Rule In or Out: decide within 60 minutes whether a security cause can be excluded, and say plainly what you know about the service-account login.
Clock Starts at Discovery: record the time the event was known or reasonably should have been known; the investigation does not need to be finished first.
Write the Reasoning: if there is no unauthorized access, record the outage as an incident with timed reasoning; do not let 'not a hack' stand as a verbal assurance.

roles.name: Public Information Officer (Director of Communications)
roles.description: Owns the standard statement for patients and families, staff intranet updates, and media and social posts about the outage, all cleared with the Incident Commander.
standingOrders: Truth Over Reassurance: say what is known, what is not known and when the next update comes; never say 'not a cyberattack' before the Privacy and Security Officer has decided.
Clear First: get the Incident Commander's approval on every statement, then make sure unit managers use the same wording at the bedside.
Answer the Rumor: respond to the hacking claims from staff, reporters and the community Facebook group with facts and a time for the next update, not with silence.

phases.title: Spinning Screens
phases.goal: Tests whether the team runs the IS-14 first hour checklist (section 4): confirming scope, declaring a downtime level under IS-14 section 3 and getting every unit onto paper procedures within 60 minutes, even though the cause is still unclear.
beats: (02:40) STARTEX: ICU, med-surg and ED charge nurses call the IS Help Desk (ext. 5500) about spinning Lakechart screens. Ananya Desai (ext. 5503) briefs that both the EHR and the interface engine have been down since 02:10, and the status dashboard shows Lakechart and the engine in red with the word DOWN. The AOC must declare a level by overhead page, the downtime hotline (ext. 5505) and the 'Downtime Alert' text group, and open the Boardroom command center (ext. 5520).

First technical note: replication to the Hermantown secondary is 40 minutes behind, so failover will not take over cleanly. The read-only downtime viewer shows 'Data current as of 23:20', so every printed census and MAR is stale by its as-of time.

The Clinical Systems Lead logs a priority-one case with the EHR vendor (contract callback within 30 minutes) and a case with the interface engine vendor (after-hours on-call callback in about 2 hours). Both case numbers go on the command board. ADT, orders, results, medication administration, charges and the MDH/HIE feeds are now queuing in their source systems, and the 8-hour hold limit runs out about 10:10.

The House Supervisor's charge-nurse calls run behind: two units have not reported a procedures time, and an unreported unit must be called after 15 minutes. Registration switches to paper and the ED registers two unidentified patients as ZZ-Trauma Tuesday 1 and 2 from the reserved record number block.

Noise item: a facilities work order for a cold-weather heat complaint in the L&D hallway, where a woman is in active labor. It is unrelated to the outage but competes for the House Supervisor's attention.

phases.title: The Odd Login
phases.goal: Tests whether the team keeps patients safe on paper while dependent work breaks down, and handles a possible security cause without deciding too early either way, inside the 60-minute rule-in/rule-out window in section 4 of the downtime policy.
beats: (03:42) The managed security provider's SOC calls the Information Security Officer about an odd login on a service account, logged at 03:30. Half the room wants Level 4 now and the other half calls it unrelated. The Security Officer must decide whether to call the cyber insurer's breach coach, and the 60-minute clock from section 4 item 6, started at the 02:40 notification, has just run out.

Effects spread to dependent work: the lab runs analyzers on green manual requisitions with DT-20270209-nnn accessions. A critical potassium of 6.9 and a positive blood culture must be phoned with read-back and entered on the Critical Result Call Log (ext. 5410) within 60 minutes. Pharmacy reports override pulls from the dispensing cabinets and a controlled-substance count that does not match. Biomed gets an ICU request to isolate the pump and monitor network.

Identity hazard on paper: med-surg finds two patients named Carlson who may share one MRN (an overlay). The Record Integrity Specialist (ext. 5431) must keep them apart on downtime labels and order sheets.

(03:55) The EHR vendor calls back 55 minutes after the case was opened, 25 minutes past its 30-minute target. It can fail over the hosted component but cannot restore the locally hosted database, which Lakemont's infrastructure team owns. It gives a 'two to three hours' estimate for the storage controller that nobody in the room believes.

The public notices: a post in a community Facebook group says 'Lakemont got hacked, my mom's nurse is writing on paper'. Staff are repeating it, and the PIO starts drafting a holding statement that must not confirm or rule out a security cause.

phases.title: Divert or Hold Open
phases.goal: Tests the exercise's one decision point. With the ED Medical Director, the AOC must decide within 2 hours whether to divert ambulances and elective admissions or keep the ED fully open on paper, and must confirm or revise the downtime level once the security question is answered.
beats: (04:40) DECISION POINT: Dr. Sofia Lindgren and the AOC must decide on diversion. Diverting sends ambulances 40+ minutes away on icy roads and loses admissions. Staying open means 22 ED patients, two ZZ-Trauma patients and new arrivals all on stale downtime reports and paper orders. The choice and its reasoning are logged on the command board.

Manual workarounds and staffing: runners are needed to hand-deliver printed lab results, and extra pharmacists are needed to reconcile the downtime medication log against cabinet overrides. The House Supervisor has to pull float staff and call in day-shift unit clerks early to keep paper flowing.

Partner friction (SimCell): the regional HIE confirms it can buffer outbound feeds for 72 hours but wants a firm timeline. MDH asks how reportable lab results will reach it, and the answer is manual reports by fax or phone. If the team diverts, the neighboring hospital that receives diverted ambulances pushes back on capacity.

(05:30) A local TV reporter calls the PIO. They have heard from staff that the hospital was hacked and give a 06:30 deadline for the morning show. Families at the bedside are asking the same question, and any statement must be cleared by the AOC.

(06:15) The Security Officer reports that the service-account login was a scheduled backup job and that the storage controller failure is the cause. The AOC must confirm Level 3 rather than Level 4 and update staff, families and the holding statement to match.

phases.title: Replay in Order
phases.goal: Tests whether the team restores in a safe order under IS-14-C. Registration (ADT) and identity checks come first, the 31,000 queued messages get a replay, hold or discard decision class by class, and Lakechart stays closed to clinicians until the lab results interface is validated. Return to normal is declared only when the IS-14-C section 6 criteria are met.
beats: (06:00 to 06:30) The interface engine vendor's on-call engineer helps promote the standby engine. Interface analysts must decide class by class (ADT, orders, results, medication administration, charges, MDH/HIE feeds) whether to replay, hold or discard the queued messages. ADT goes first and every replay passes the identity check. Stale orders for patients discharged overnight must be held, and the 10:10 queue-drop limit is close.

Hurdle: the ED Medical Director asks to open Lakechart to clinicians now, before the LIS-to-EHR interface has been validated. The chart would look complete but be missing overnight results, and IS-14-A section 3 forbids releasing results until validation. During the first replay, the ZZ-Trauma and Carlson records fail to match the master patient index and need manual merge decisions.

Looking ahead (the 14:00 restore estimate falls after ENDEX): when the infrastructure team brings the locally hosted Lakechart database back from the replaced storage controller, the HIM Director will give hourly reconciliation counts by unit, covering paper orders back-entered, duplicate records created from the reserved MRN block, and results reprinted for the chart.

Verification before trust: interfaces must run stable for 2 hours, every unit must report ready, there must be no critical open items, and a final staff message goes out (IS-14-C section 6). The PIO issues a final public update saying the cause was an equipment failure and not an attack.

The Clinical Systems Lead lists the after-action measures from IS-14-C section 8: time to declaration, time until all units were on procedures, late critical results, duplicates, the restore order used and the notification clocks met. A hot wash is set within 14 days, followed by ENDEX.

msel.event: STARTEX CARD (EXERCISE: all patients and record numbers are fictional). It is 02:40 on Tuesday, February 9, 2027, in Duluth. Clear sky, -21°F, wind chill near -40°F. Census: 98 inpatients, 22 patients in the ED, one woman in active labor on L&D. Lakechart and the interface engine were normal (green, OK) at the 02:00 check. Since 02:14 the IS Help Desk (ext. 5500) has logged calls from the ICU, med-surg and ED charge nurses: "Lakechart is just spinning, we can't open a chart or scan a med." At 02:25 on-call analyst Ananya Desai (ext. 5503) confirmed the problem. She now phones the Administrator on Call: "Both the EHR and the interface engine have been down since 02:10. The IC records that a step-down to Level 3 comes only once the standby engine is live and a security cause has been ruled out. The House Supervisor calls each charge nurse to start IS-14-A procedures.

objectiveCapabilities.why: The Administrator on Call, acting as Incident Commander, has to declare the Lakechart downtime level, open the Boardroom command center and later confirm or change the level. The IC also has to decide on diversion with the ED Medical Director within 2 hours (IS-14 sections 3 and 4).
Choosing Level 3 or Level 4 depends on whether the Security Officer rules a security cause in or out within the 60-minute window after the unexplained 03:30 svc-rptexport login.

Patients have to be kept safe on paper under IS-14-A. That means manual lab requisitions, phoning critical results with read-back and logging them within 60 minutes, labelling specimens with downtime identifiers, and keeping the ZZ-Trauma and Carlson identities apart.
The House Supervisor has to get every unit onto downtime procedures within 60 minutes of declaration, record when each unit reports, and call any unit that has not reported after 15 minutes.

The Clinical Systems Lead runs the technical recovery with Northpine and Relaywell, decides replay, hold or discard for each message class under IS-14-C section 2, and keeps Lakechart closed until the identity check and the lab results interface are validated (IS-14-C section 1).
The PIO has to issue staff, family and media statements that the IC has cleared, answering the 'hacked' claims without getting ahead of the Security Officer's decision (IS-14 section 8).
Public wording about the cause depends on the Security Officer's timed rule-in/rule-out decision and the HIPAA breach risk assessment.

hotwash.methodDescription: Ask the room for three things that went well and three things that broke or failed during the Lakechart outage. Go around the room one team at a time (command, IS, clinical, lab/pharmacy, communications), write every item on the whiteboard in two columns, and don't debate any item until all teams have spoken.

questions.text: At I-01 (02:49), Ananya told you the downtime viewer banner read 'Data current as of 23:20' and that every census and MAR was 3 hr 20 min old. When did you stop trusting those printouts, and what did you tell the units to do about the missing 00:00 and 02:00 med passes and the patients admitted after 23:20? Did anyone treat the viewer as current because it was 'up'?

From 03:30 to 06:15 the service-account login was unexplained. Under the First Hour Checklist, item 6, that meant handling it as a suspected security incident after 60 minutes. Did you declare Level 3 or Level 4, who decided, and did you revise the level when I-15 showed RPTEXPORT-NIGHTLY-BKP was to blame and that controller A failed 80 minutes before the login? What would have let you make that call faster?

At I-12, Dr. Sofia Lindgren asked you to divert or stay open. You had two D-number traumas with a crossmatch pending, a STEMI 12 minutes out, and a 40-plus-minute route on icy Highway 61 to North Shore Bluffs, which was at 94 percent. What did you decide, did you make it inside the 2-hour window, and how much did hearing from the receiving hospital change your choice?

The engine held 31,000 queued messages, and source systems could hold them for only 8 hours. Did you decide replay, hold or discard for each message class, starting with ADT and logging each decision? Who refused to open Lakechart to clinicians before the lab results interface was validated? And how did you keep the ZZ-Trauma and D-number identities from colliding with replayed results?

Staff, a local TV reporter and a Facebook post were calling this a hack, and at I-12b the HIE wanted a firm restore time by 08:00 while MDH asked how reportable results like the positive blood culture would reach them. What did you say publicly and to partners before you knew the cause? Did the Incident Commander clear every statement, and did you avoid confirming or ruling out a security cause before the Security Officer decided?

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Northpine EHR priority-one support (senior engineer Dale Rusk, case P1-20270209-0417) and Relaywell Integration after-hours on-call engineer (ticket RW-88213): the vendors whose services are down
simcellScripts.trigger: The Clinical Systems Lead opens or chases a case. Northpine answers through I-02 and calls back at I-08. Relaywell calls back at I-16/I-17. Also triggered when any player asks a vendor to 'just fix it' or to release queued messages.
hardQuestions: Northpine: "What's your case number? I've got three P1s tonight. Who's your named technical contact, and is your infrastructure team actually on the array right now? I can't touch a database that sits in your data center."

Northpine: "You want the hosted web and print failover? I need that request in writing from someone authorized to sign for Lakemont, plus a site contact and dock access for the hardware tech. Who signs?"
Relaywell: "I've got about 31,000 messages in my store. I won't release a single channel until you tell me replay, hold or discard for each class, in writing, with a name on it. Which goes first?"
Relaywell: "138 of those orders belong to patients you've discharged or moved since 23:20, and about 700 are already done on paper. Do you want me to replay them anyway? Your call, not mine."
concessions: Northpine runs the hosted web and printing failover, and pushes the hardware partner for a firm arrival time, once the case number is logged and a written authorization with a named site contact is received.
Relaywell releases ADT first and holds every other class, once the CSL gives a written decision for each class with the decision-maker named.
Relaywell exports the list of stale orders and results for the 6 discharged or transferred patients, so they can be discarded with a count, once the team says who will reconcile them.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Regional health information exchange operations desk and the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) infectious disease epidemiologist: partner agencies that depend on Lakemont's outbound feeds
simcellScripts.trigger: I-12b arrives, or the CSL or LPM contacts the HIE or MDH about the silent ADT, results and ELR feeds. Also triggered if no one has told partners about the outage by 04:30.
hardQuestions: HIE: "Your feed has been silent since 02:10. I can buffer 72 hours, but three member hospitals and two care-coordination programs want a restore time by 08:00 for our partner bulletin. 'Unknown' won't satisfy them. What do I tell them?"
HIE: "When you replay, are you sending me stale orders and duplicate registrations? I don't want your D-numbers spreading through the exchange."
MDH: "Our ELR queue from you went quiet at 02:10. You have a positive blood culture working up. How are reportable results getting to me tonight? Who is phoning or faxing them, and when?"
MDH: "Is this a significant disruption to patient care? Nobody from Lakemont has told the department yet."
concessions: The HIE accepts a 'next update by' time instead of a restore time, and holds the buffer, once the CSL commits to a named contact and an update schedule.
The HIE agrees to hold ingestion of replayed ADT until Lakemont confirms its identity check passed, if asked.
MDH accepts manual case reports by phone or fax through the reporting portal, and takes the Laboratory Manager's callback number, once a named person is assigned to report.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Duluth dispatch (St. Louis County ambulance routing) and the North Shore Bluffs Medical Center house supervisor
simcellScripts.trigger: I-12, the diversion decision point. Also triggered at any time a player says 'we go on diversion' or 'call the neighbors.'
hardQuestions: Dispatch: "Lakemont, yes or no on diversion? I have a chest pain with ST changes 12 minutes out. If you divert, he goes to North Shore Bluffs, 40-plus minutes tonight with the ice on 61. Is that what you want?"
Dispatch: "Diversion for what, and until when? Everything, or just electives? When do you reassess? I need a time."
North Shore Bluffs: "We're at 94 percent with four boarders and a CT down. I'll take criticals, not a steady stream and not your electives. Who's your physician-to-physician contact if I accept one?"
concessions: Dispatch accepts a limited diversion (electives only, or specific categories) with a reassessment time and a callback number.
North Shore Bluffs accepts named critical transfers with a physician-to-physician call, once Lakemont confirms what records travel with the patient while the EHR is down.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Northstar Managed Security SOC analyst (ticket NSM-27-00562) and Harborline Cyber Risk breach coach (the cyber insurer's counsel panel)
simcellScripts.trigger: The SOC calls at I-07 and updates at I-15. The breach coach calls at I-18. Also triggered when the Security Officer or IC asks either party about breach status or about disabling svc-rptexport.
hardQuestions: SOC: "Do you want svc-rptexport disabled, yes or no? I need that from the Security Officer by name. If I kill it and it's your backup job, that's on you."
SOC: "Have you preserved the event logs on the Hermantown host and the array? If someone pulls hardware before you've captured them, I can't tell you anything later."

Breach coach: "Before anyone says 'breach': was there unauthorized access to PHI, yes or no, and on what evidence? If yes, discovery was overnight and the clock is running. If no, write down why and when you decided."
Breach coach: "Your infrastructure team wants to ship the failed controller. Did security clear that, and is it in your decision log?"
concessions: The SOC disables or watches the account on the Security Officer's written order, and sends the full correlation (I-15) once asked for evidence, not reassurance.

The breach coach accepts a documented 'security cause ruled out' determination, with the evidence, time and decision-maker, and agrees no HIPAA notification clock is triggered on these facts. This may support compliance; the compliance office decides.
The breach coach approves removal of the failed controller once the logs are confirmed preserved and the release is logged.

simcellScripts.trigger: I-14 (phone slip at 05:30) and I-19 (call at 06:31 after the live chyron). Also triggered if the PIO calls the station first.
hardQuestions: "We're hearing from several of your staff that you were hacked. Was it a cyberattack, yes or no? We go live at 06:30 and we'll run it with or without you."
"Were patient records exposed? Is the ER open right now? If ambulances are being sent elsewhere, people need to know that this morning."
"Can I get that on the record from a named spokesperson? 'We're looking into it' means I say you declined again at 7:00."
"Your own nurses are telling families 'probably.' Why should viewers believe you over them?"

The producer updates the chyron and online story away from 'hack' when given a clear, attributable statement of what is known, what is not known and when the next update comes.
The producer agrees to a scheduled follow-up call time instead of door-stepping staff, if the PIO gives a direct number and commits to an update time.

assumptions: The exercise is conducted in a no-fault learning environment. The aim is to test Lakemont's downtime plans and decisions, not to grade individual staff.

The scenario is plausible, and events occur as they are presented. Players accept the overnight conditions as given: the cold, the icy roads, the census, the queue counts and the vendor response times.

Players respond in accordance with existing plans, policies and procedures, including the Downtime Policy (IS-14), the Downtime Procedures SOP (IS-14-A) and the Restore and Reconciliation SOP (IS-14-C). Where a plan is silent, players say so and state what they would do.
Players know only what has been presented to them in the injects and module updates. They do not assume the cause of the outage or any outcome that has not been presented.
Decisions made in one module carry into the next unless the facilitator says otherwise.
All patients, record numbers, accession numbers and ticket numbers are fictional.
artificialities: Time is compressed. Each module covers one hour of exercise time, and the facilitator's time-jump cards move the clock forward between modules (02:40, 03:40, 04:40 and 05:40, ending at 06:40).

The SimCell plays everyone outside the Boardroom. That includes the on-call analyst, the Northpine EHR vendor and its hardware partner, the Relaywell interface engine vendor, the Northstar SOC, the cyber insurer's breach coach, the regional HIE, the Minnesota Department of Health, ambulance dispatch, North Shore Bluffs Medical Center, unit staff, families, Northland 6 News and the community Facebook groups.

Lakechart, the interface engine, the storage array, the downtime viewer, the dispensing cabinets, the LIS and the medical device network are named as they are in the plans, but nobody touches them. No account is disabled, no network is isolated and no message is released.

Injects arrive on paper cards or on screen: status boards, emails, tickets, social media posts and a news chyron. Players simulate phone calls to people who are not in the room, and the command board stands in for the real one.

**Module 1: Spinning Screens (02:40–03:40)**

It is 02:40 on Tuesday, February 9, 2027, in Duluth. The sky is clear, it is -21°F and the wind chill is near -40°F. The census is 98 inpatients and 22 patients in the ED, plus one woman in active labor on L&D. At the 02:00 check, Lakechart and the interface engine were both green.

At 02:25 the on-call analyst confirmed the problem, and she is now on the phone with the Administrator on Call. Both the EHR and the interface engine have been down since 02:10, and the status dashboard shows LAKECHART PROD and INTERFACE ENGINE both RED (DOWN). The cause is not known. The Clinical Systems Lead and the CMIO are driving in, and **nobody has declared a downtime level yet.**

Getting every unit onto paper procedures within 60 minutes of the declaration

Getting the laboratory and pharmacy into a known manual state within 30 minutes

**Module 2: The Odd Login (03:40–04:40)**

It is 03:40. Lakechart and the interface engine are still RED (DOWN), 90 minutes after the 02:10 failure. The on-call analyst has reported that controller A on the primary storage array is in FAULT and controller B has not taken over the Lakechart database volume. Replication to the Hermantown secondary stopped about 40 minutes behind, at roughly 01:30. The downtime viewer is up, but its data is current only as of 23:20, so printed censuses and MARs miss the 00:00 and 02:00 med passes and everyone admitted or moved since then. The Northpine Priority 1 case was opened at 03:00 with a 30-minute callback target. Relaywell's after-hours line says to expect a callback in about two hours.

The interface monitor shows about 9,535 messages held at source, and the source hold limit runs out at about 10:10. Every cabinet is in override, the Core Lab is working from paper requisitions, and runners are carrying green slips. At 03:15 the House Supervisor's tracker showed ICU, ED, Med-Surg Level 3 and L&D on procedures, with Pediatrics and Behavioral Health not yet reported. Two unidentified Highway 53 rollover patients were registered on paper as ZZ-Trauma Tuesday 1 (D-004117) and ZZ-Trauma Tuesday 2 (D-004118), and blood bank has a crossmatch request for both. The L&D hallway is at 61°F and falling with a patient in active labor. A community Facebook post saying the hospital was "HACKED" is spreading.

The Clinical Systems Lead is now in the Boardroom (ext. 5520), and the CMIO is about 20 minutes out. **No one has yet said whether this could be a security event.**

Phoning critical results safely when the census is 3+ hours old
Keeping the D-numbered trauma patients' identities separate until they can be matched

modules.narrativeMd:
**Module 3: Divert or Hold Open (04:40–05:40)**

It is 04:40. Lakechart and the interface engine have been RED (DOWN) for 2 hours 30 minutes, the temperature is still -21°F and the roads are glazed. The CMIO is now in the Boardroom. At 03:42 the managed security provider reported a high-severity alert. At 03:30, service account svc-rptexport made an interactive remote logon from a host on the Hermantown segment. The account had not logged on interactively in 90 days, and the logon failed 14 times before it succeeded. The SOC could not say whether the logon is related to the outage, and it **remains unexplained**. A biomedical technician has asked who can order the ICU pump and monitor network isolated.

The Northpine engineer called back 55 minutes after the case was opened. He said Lakemont must restore its own database and that a replacement controller has no firm arrival time. The array log shows controller A FAULT at 02:09:52 and controller B takeover ABORTED at 02:10:07. Relaywell has not called back. About 15,890 messages are held at source, and the source hold runs out at about 10:10.

On the floors, the lab has a critical potassium of 6.9 on a patient who was moved to ICU at 01:15, after the census was printed, and a positive blood culture on an ICU patient. Neither had read-back at 04:05. The ICU hydromorphone count is one vial short, and Med-Surg has two patients named Carlson sharing one MRN on their labels. The ED has 25 patients, including the two ZZ-Trauma patients. A second Facebook post says "Lakemont got hacked," and a nurse manager needs words for the 05:00 rounds. **The downtime level is provisional, and the 2-hour window for the diversion decision is closing.**

**Module 4: Replay in Order (05:40–06:40)**

It is 05:40. Lakechart has been RED (DOWN) for 3 hours 30 minutes, and the day shift is fighting icy roads to arrive by 07:00. The ambulance decision made at 04:45 stands. At 05:38 the SOC reported that the 03:30 svc-rptexport logon matches the Hermantown backup job RPTEXPORT-NIGHTLY-BKP. Its fallback script opened an interactive session after the database connection failed, and the SOC found no other hosts, no new processes and no outbound transfer. The on-call analyst notes that controller A failed at 02:09:52, 80 minutes before the logon. **No one has yet formally said whether a security cause is ruled out**, so the downtime level is still provisional.

The Relaywell engineer called back at 05:10 and is promoting the standby interface engine at 06:00. About 22,240 messages are held at source: ADT 291, orders 3,780, results 8,820, medication administration 5,460, charges 3,680, and ELR, immunizations and HIE outbound 210. The source hold runs out at about 10:10. A replacement storage controller is on the road from the Twin Cities. HIM has opened a paper reconciliation tracker, and downtime numbers D-004112 to D-004124 have been issued. Paper orders waiting for back-entry total 595 across the units. Northland 6 News has called about "hack" reports and goes live at 06:30, with or without a comment from Lakemont.
